chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi 'Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
"When a man accuses his wife (of adultery), he does not undergo li'an (mutual imprecation) until he says: 'I saw between her legs a man having intercourse with her.'
He said: And he was asked about the man who accuses his wife, he said: 'He undergoes li'an with her, then they are separated, and she is not permissible to him ever.'
If he confesses against himself before the li'an, he is flogged with the hadd penalty, and she remains his wife.
And he said: And I asked him about the free woman whom her husband accuses, and he is a slave, he said: 'He undergoes li'an with her.'

He said: And I asked him about the li'an in which her husband accuses her, denies his paternity of her child, undergoes li'an with her, and divorces her, then after that the child says: 'He is my father,' and he denies himself, so he said: 'As for the woman, she does not return to him ever.
As for the child, I return him to him if he claims him, and I do not leave his child.
And he has no inheritance (from the child), and the son inherits the father, and the father does not inherit the son.
And his inheritance belongs to his maternal uncles. If his father does not claim him, then his maternal uncles inherit him, and they do not inherit from him.
And if anyone claims him, saying: 'O son of the fornicator,' he is flogged with the hadd penalty.'
Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: And this report indicates that li'an occurs between the slave and the free woman, and to add clarification to that is what he narrated:
ai.seo_question: What are the legal consequences of li'an between a husband and wife in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Tusi's *Tahdhib* clarifies the procedural nuances of li'an, emphasizing that the husband must specify seeing a specific man to trigger the ritual, and establishes that the resulting separation is permanent. It further details the complex inheritance dynamics where the child inherits from the maternal uncles (akhwal) but not the father, reflecting the Shia juristic view of paternity denial through li'an. The text also addresses the universality of li'an across social statuses, confirming it applies equally between a free woman and an enslaved husband.
